We begin supervised learning with one of the simplest techniques, linear regression, which we use to show the power of Bayesian inference. The method is conceptually straightforward, yet it shows surprising mathematical depth when we view it through Bayesian inference. By treating both the data and the model parameters as random variables, we gain a fuller statistical understanding of the fitting process.

We choose linear regression for two reasons. Its simplicity gives an ideal setting to visualize Bayesian inference in action, because line fitting makes abstract statistical concepts concrete and practical. Its capabilities and limitations also lead to many other concepts in machine learning. What we learn here extends to more sophisticated methods, from logistic regression to Gaussian processes and neural networks in later chapters.

4.1 Linear Regression Fundamentals

Linear regression maps an input variable \(x\) to a continuous output variable \(y\) through a linear relationship. In its basic form, the relationship is \[ y = w_0 + w_1x, \] where \(w_0\) is the intercept and \(w_1\) is the slope. This equation embodies a strong inductive bias, an assumption about the relationship we want to model. Here we assume that \(x\) and \(y\) are linearly related.

Linear regression may seem too restrictive, because many astronomical phenomena are nonlinear. Yet it remains widely used in astronomical research, for three reasons that show the power of “keeping things simple” while keeping the mathematics sound.

Expressiveness Through Transformations

We can make linear regression surprisingly expressive by transforming the input features, the quantities that the model uses to predict \(y\). For example, Kepler’s Third Law relates the orbital period (\(P\)) to the semi-major axis (\(a\)) of an orbit around a mass \(M\) through the equation \[ P^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM}a^3. \] This nonlinear relationship becomes linear when we take logarithms of both sides \[ \log P = \frac{1}{2}\log\left(\frac{4\pi^2}{GM}\right) + \frac{3}{2}\log a. \]

The transformation technique is especially useful because many basic relationships in astronomy follow power laws. As we discussed in Chapter 2, power laws appear when physical processes operate similarly at different scales, meaning that the system has no preferred scale. This scale invariance appears in systems from stellar masses to galaxy properties, so power laws are common in our field.

Consider the M-\(\sigma\) relation, which links the mass of a supermassive black hole (\(M_{\rm BH}\)) to the velocity dispersion (\(\sigma_\star\)) of its host galaxy’s bulge \[ M_{\rm BH} = A \sigma_\star^\gamma. \] Similarly, the Kennicutt-Schmidt law relates the star formation rate surface density (\(\Sigma_{\rm SFR}\)) to the gas surface density (\(\Sigma_{\rm gas}\)) \[ \Sigma_{\rm SFR} = A \Sigma_{\rm gas}^\gamma. \]Both relationships are nonlinear in their original form, but they become linear in logarithmic space \[ \log M_{\rm BH} = \log A + \gamma \log \sigma_\star, \] \[ \log \Sigma_{\rm SFR} = \log A + \gamma \log \Sigma_{\rm gas}. \]

Physical Interpretability

These examples show one advantage of linear regression, which is that its models are often easier to interpret physically than more complex approaches. The coefficients, or weights in modern machine learning terminology, correspond to physically meaningful quantities. The slope \(\gamma\) in these logarithmic relationships is the power-law index, which tells us about the underlying physics. For instance, in the Kennicutt-Schmidt law, \(\gamma \approx 1.4\) means a superlinear relationship, so doubling the gas density more than doubles the star formation rate. This suggests that star formation becomes more efficient at higher gas densities. Stronger self-gravity and more frequent molecular cloud collisions in denser environments may explain this.

The intercept (\(\log A\)) also carries physical meaning. In the M-\(\sigma\) relation, \(\log A\) is the normalization that connects stellar dynamics to black hole mass. In the Kennicutt-Schmidt law, it measures the global efficiency of star formation. This says how effectively a galaxy turns a given density of molecular gas into new stars.

Mathematical Advantages

Linear regression also has mathematical advantages that follow from Bayesian inference. First, for many objective functions derived from Bayesian inference, it has analytical solutions. We can then find the best model parameters by direct calculation, with no computationally expensive iterative optimization. Second, it fits the Bayesian view of the model parameters as random variables. This lets us quantify the full probability distribution of the parameters, which goes beyond a point estimate. It gives the parameter uncertainties and their correlations, which scientific inference needs.

4.2 Mathematical Formalism

We assume that the output \(y\) is a scalar, such as a single black hole mass. It is a linear combination of the input features plus a noise term \(\varepsilon\). With \(D\) input features, we can write this explicitly as \[ y = w_0 + w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + \ldots + w_Dx_D + \varepsilon. \]

For mathematical convenience, we can absorb the intercept \(w_0\) into the weight vector by adding a constant 1 to the feature vector \[ \begin{pmatrix} y \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} w_0 & w_1 & w_2 & \cdots & w_D \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ x_1 \\ x_2 \\ \vdots \\ x_D \end{pmatrix} + \varepsilon. \] With this constant as the first feature, \(w_0\) becomes part of the weight vector. We write \(\mathbf{w} = (w_0, w_1, \ldots, w_D)^T\) and \(\mathbf{x} = (1, x_1, \ldots, x_D)^T\). The single dot product \(\mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x}\) then expresses both the linear transformation and the intercept. This is mathematically equivalent to the explicit form, so we can write the model compactly in vector notation \[ y = \mathbf{w}^T \mathbf{x} + \varepsilon. \]

The vector \(\mathbf{w}\) holds the model parameters (weights), and \(\varepsilon\) represents the noise or error in our measurements. The intercept \(w_0\) is also called the bias term. It lets the model shift its predictions up or down, independent of the input features. This constant offset differs from the inductive bias of Section 4.1.

For example, take the M-\(\sigma\) relation after taking logarithms. In its simplest form, \(y\) is \(\log M_{\rm BH}\) and \(x_1\) is \(\log \sigma_\star\). Here \(\sigma_\star\) is the velocity dispersion and differs from the noise level \(\sigma\) of Section 4.3. We can add other features that might influence black hole mass, such as galaxy morphology indicators or environmental parameters, which makes \(\mathbf{x}\) multidimensional. For instance, we might model \[ \log M_{\rm BH} = w_0 + w_1\log \sigma_\star + w_2\log R_e + w_3(B/T) + \varepsilon, \] where \(R_e\) is the effective radius of the galaxy and \(B/T\) is the bulge-to-total mass ratio. Here \(w_0\) is the baseline value of \(\log M_{\rm BH}\) when all other terms are zero.

The model generalizes to vector-valued outputs, such as predicting several galaxy properties at once. We then use a separate set of weights \(\mathbf{w}_k\) for each output dimension \(y_k\), which amounts to running several regressions in parallel.

We also need not use the raw input features directly. As the power-law examples showed, we can apply transformations of our choice and map \(\mathbf{x}\) to a new feature space through functions \(\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})\). This gives a more general form of linear regression \[ y(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) = \sum_{j=0}^{M-1} w_j \cdot \phi_j(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w}^T \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}), \] where \(\mathbf{w} = (w_0, \ldots, w_{M-1})^T\) is the vector of parameters and \(\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}) = (\phi_0(\mathbf{x}), \ldots, \phi_{M-1}(\mathbf{x}))^T\) is the vector of basis functions. By convention, \(\phi_0(\mathbf{x}) = 1\), which is the constant first feature from above. Each basis function is a fixed function of the input, and the model takes a weighted sum of them.

The notation \(y(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w})\) stresses that the model is a function. It maps an input \(\mathbf{x}\) to a predicted output \(y\) for given parameters \(\mathbf{w}\). This functional view matters because our goal is to find parameters \(\mathbf{w}\) that fit the existing data and also predict new, unseen data accurately.

In the M-\(\sigma\) example, suitable parameters \(\mathbf{w}\) let us estimate the black hole mass of a galaxy from its velocity dispersion and other properties. This predictive view, which turns data into insight that generalizes beyond the training set, is central to machine learning. The training set is the data that we use to fit the model (Section 4.7).

The basis functions \(\phi_j(\mathbf{x})\) can take many forms. In our power-law examples, \(\phi_1(\mathbf{x})\) might be \(\log(x)\). For polynomial regression, we might use \(\phi_j(\mathbf{x}) = x^j\). When we simply take \(\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}\), we recover our original linear regression form.

The choice of basis functions is an important design decision. It lets us encode domain knowledge about the expected relationships in our data. The model stays linear in the parameters \(\mathbf{w}\), which keeps the mathematical advantages of linearity. This is why “linear” regression can be nonlinear in the input features. For example, \(w_0 + w_1x + w_2x^2\) is linear in \(w_0\), \(w_1\) and \(w_2\).

4.3 Maximum Likelihood Estimation

Having defined the model, we ask what makes a set of parameters \(\mathbf{w}\) “best” for our purposes. We want parameters that fit the existing data and also generalize to new observations. We can formalize this balance with Bayesian inference.

Recall from Chapter 2 that we use \(\boldsymbol{\theta}\) for the model parameters in general Bayesian inference. For linear regression we use \(\mathbf{w}\) for the weight parameters, following the machine learning convention. The posterior distribution of the parameters is proportional to the product of the likelihood and the prior \[ p(\mathbf{w}|\mathcal{D}) \propto p(\mathcal{D}|\mathbf{w})p(\mathbf{w}). \] Here \(\mathbf{w}\) is itself a random variable, and the posterior gives its probability distribution. The posterior describes our uncertainty about the true parameter values, given the data \(\mathcal{D}\). It tells us the most likely parameter values and also how confident we can be in them.

The complete distribution is informative, but we often want a single “best” set of parameters. One common choice maximizes the posterior probability \[ \mathbf{w}_{\text{MAP}} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{w}} p(\mathbf{w}|\mathcal{D}). \] This is the Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimate. Here \(\arg\max_{\mathbf{w}}\) is the value of \(\mathbf{w}\) at which the function that follows is largest. Similarly, \(\arg\min\) is the value at which it is smallest. We start with the simpler case of minimal prior knowledge, a so-called uninformative prior, and we take \(p(\mathbf{w})\) to be approximately constant. Maximizing the posterior is then equivalent to maximizing the likelihood \(p(\mathcal{D}|\mathbf{w})\) alone \[ \mathbf{w}_{\text{ML}} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{w}} p(\mathcal{D}|\mathbf{w}). \] This approach is maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), the simplest way to choose parameters, based purely on how well they explain the observed data.

The Gaussian Likelihood

The likelihood \(p(\mathcal{D}|\mathbf{w})\) asks how likely we are to observe our actual data, given a proposed set of parameters \(\mathbf{w}\), which MLE optimizes. Our data are pairs \((\mathbf{x}_i, t_i)\), where \(t_i\) is an observed value.

We assume that each observation relates to the model prediction as \[ t = y(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) + \varepsilon, \text{ where } \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2). \] Here we deliberately distinguish between \(t\), the observed value, and \(y(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w})\), the deterministic model prediction for input \(\mathbf{x}\) and parameters \(\mathbf{w}\). In Section 4.2, \(y\) included the noise \(\varepsilon\), but from here on only the observed value \(t\) includes it. This noise follows a Gaussian distribution centered at zero with variance \(\sigma^2\). It states our assumption that measurements scatter symmetrically around the true model values because of random uncertainties.

This treatment of uncertainty is more than a mathematical convenience, because it is necessary for meaningful Bayesian inference. If our data were perfectly certain (\(\sigma = 0\)), we would expect to know the model parameters with perfect precision. This does not occur in real astronomical observations. As we discussed in Chapter 2, the precision of our measurements limits our understanding of physical systems. This is why we need Bayesian statistics, to quantify and reason about these unavoidable uncertainties.

For a single observation, the likelihood of observing value \(t\) at input \(\mathbf{x}\) follows from our noise model. Because \(t = y(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) + \varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\), the observation \(t\) itself follows a Gaussian distribution centered at the model prediction \(y(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w})\) with variance \(\sigma^2\). We can write this explicitly with the Gaussian probability density function \[\begin{align*} p(t | \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}, \sigma^2) &= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \exp\left(-\frac{(t - y(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}))^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \\ &= \mathcal{N}(t | y(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}), \sigma^2). \tag{4.18} \end{align*}\]

This equation formalizes our belief about where observations fall relative to the model predictions. The parameter \(\sigma^2\) sets how quickly the probability falls off. Larger values of \(\sigma^2\) mean greater measurement uncertainty and a more gradual decrease in probability away from the model prediction. With small \(\sigma^2\) and the correct parameters \(\mathbf{w}\), we expect the observations to cluster tightly around the model predictions, while larger \(\sigma^2\) allows more scatter.

With incorrect parameters, we expect systematic deviations, where the predictions consistently miss the data points even after we account for measurement uncertainties. The Gaussians centered on the model predictions then fail to match the pattern of the observations, which tells us to adjust the model parameters.

Figure 4.1 shows the likelihood for good and poor model parameters. The dotted lines mark the residuals, the differences between the observations and the model predictions. In panel (a), the model predictions agree with the data within the expected uncertainties. In panel (b), they systematically miss the observations, which indicates poorly chosen parameters. By maximizing the likelihood, we expect the parameters to converge to values whose predictions best explain the observations, given the known measurement uncertainties.

Next, we consider \(N\) data points instead of one. We assume that the observations are independent, so knowing the outcome of one measurement tells us nothing about the others. In the M-\(\sigma\) relation, for example, the velocity dispersion we measure for one galaxy does not influence our measurement for another galaxy. This is often a reasonable assumption in astronomy, where we typically observe different objects in separate observations, each with its own random measurement uncertainties.

We also allow each measurement to have a different uncertainty \(\sigma_i^2\). The likelihood of the dataset is the product of the individual likelihoods. This follows because independent events occur together with a probability equal to the product of their individual probabilities. Here \(\mathbf{t}\) is the vector of all observed target values and \(\mathbf{X}\) is the matrix of input features, with one row per data point \[ p(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{w}, \{\sigma_i^2\}) = \prod_{i=1}^N p(t_i | \mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{w}, \sigma_i^2) = \prod_{i=1}^N \mathcal{N}(t_i | \mathbf{w}^T \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_i), \sigma_i^2). \]This product form combines the evidence from multiple independent measurements and weights each observation by its own uncertainty \(\sigma_i^2\).

To make the product easier to handle, we take the logarithm of both sides. The logarithm is a monotonic function, meaning that it preserves the order of numbers, so maximizing the log-likelihood is equivalent to maximizing the likelihood itself. It also converts the product of probabilities into a sum, which is much easier to work with \[ \ln p(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{w}, \{\sigma_i^2\}) = \sum_{i=1}^N \ln \mathcal{N}(t_i | \mathbf{w}^T \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_i), \sigma_i^2). \]Expanding this with the explicit form of the Gaussian distribution and heterogeneous noise gives \[ \ln p(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{w}, \{\sigma_i^2\}) = -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^N \ln\left(2\pi\sigma_i^2\right) - \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{\left(t_i - \mathbf{w}^T \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_i)\right)^2}{2\sigma_i^2}. \]

Weighted Least Squares

To find the parameters \(\mathbf{w}\) that maximize this log-likelihood, we need only the terms that depend on \(\mathbf{w}\). The first term does not depend on \(\mathbf{w}\), so we drop it and minimize the negative of the second term \[ \arg\max_\mathbf{w} \ln p(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{w}, \{\sigma_i^2\}) = \arg\min_\mathbf{w} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{(t_i - \mathbf{w}^T \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_i))^2}{2\sigma_i^2}. \]This equation shows that maximizing the likelihood under heterogeneous Gaussian noise is equivalent to minimizing the weighted sum of squared errors. The weights are inversely proportional to the measurement variances, so more precise measurements (smaller \(\sigma_i^2\)) contribute more to the optimal parameters. These data weights differ from the model weights \(\mathbf{w}\), the parameters that we fit. When \(\sigma_i^2\) varies, which we call heteroscedastic errors, standard unweighted least squares would wrongly give equal weight to all measurements, whatever their precision.

For homogeneous noise, where \(\sigma_i = \sigma\) for all \(i\), which we call homoscedastic, the equation simplifies to \[ \arg\min_\mathbf{w} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{(t_i - \mathbf{w}^T \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_i))^2}{2\sigma^2} = \frac{1}{2\sigma^2} \arg\min_\mathbf{w} \sum_{i=1}^N (t_i - \mathbf{w}^T \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_i))^2. \]Since \(1/(2\sigma^2)\) is a constant scaling factor, minimizing this expression is equivalent to minimizing the unweighted sum of squared errors. This explains why standard least squares is appropriate when the measurement uncertainties are uniform.

We have seen that weighted least squares emerges from maximum likelihood estimation once we account for the measurement uncertainties. Up to a factor of 2, the weighted sum of squared residuals that we derived is \(\sum_{i=1}^N (t_i - \mathbf{w}^T \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_i))^2/\sigma_i^2\), the chi-square statistic, written \(\chi^2\). It measures the goodness of fit between the model predictions and the data, with each squared residual weighted by its measurement uncertainty. Chi-square is widely used in astronomical model fitting. This is no arbitrary choice, since chi-square is a direct mathematical consequence of the Gaussian noise model.

4.4 Analytical Solution

The quantity that we minimize to fit the model is the loss function, also called the objective function. To find the optimal parameters \(\mathbf{w}\), we start from our weighted least squares loss function \[ E(\mathbf{w}) = \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{(t_i - \mathbf{w}^T \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_i))^2}{2\sigma_i^2}. \] It can be rewritten in matrix form \[ E(\mathbf{w}) = \frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{t} - \boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w})^T \mathbf{S}^{-1} (\mathbf{t} - \boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w}). \] Here \(\mathbf{t} = (t_1, \ldots, t_N)^T \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 1}\) is the vector of observed values and \(N\) is the number of data points. The matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Phi} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times M}\) is the design matrix of regression analysis. It stacks the features of all data points, so that \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w}\) is the vector of the \(N\) model predictions. Each row corresponds to one data point, and each column corresponds to one feature or predictor variable. The entry at row \(i\) and column \(j\) is the \(j\)th feature evaluated at the \(i\)th data point.

More formally, \(\boldsymbol{\Phi} = [\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_1), \ldots, \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_N)]^T\), where \(\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})\) holds the feature transformations (also called basis functions) that map each input \(\mathbf{x}\) to an \(M\)-dimensional feature vector. For a quadratic fit, for example, \(\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})\) maps a single input \(x\) to the vector \((1, x, x^2)\), so \(M=3\). For two input points \(x_1\) and \(x_2\), \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\) is \[ \boldsymbol{\Phi} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & x_1 & x_1^2 \\ 1 & x_2 & x_2^2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, \(\mathbf{S} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}\) is the diagonal matrix of measurement variances, \(\text{diag}(\sigma_1^2, \ldots, \sigma_N^2)\), where \(\sigma_i^2\) is the variance of the \(i\)th measurement. Its inverse is also diagonal, with elements \(1/\sigma_i^2\), so \(\mathbf{S}^{-1} = \text{diag}(1/\sigma_1^2, \ldots, 1/\sigma_N^2)\).

Deriving the Solution

The quadratic form has two important properties, familiar from simple quadratics such as \(y = ax^2 + bx + c\). First, the function is convex (it opens upward when \(a > 0\)), so it has one global minimum, like a parabola with exactly one lowest point. Second, we can find the minimum analytically by “completing the square”, a technique from basic algebra that rewrites \(ax^2 + bx + c\) as \(a(x + b/(2a))^2 + (c - b^2/(4a))\) to reveal the vertex. The same principle applies here, in higher dimensions.

We could complete the square, but taking derivatives is more direct and efficient to compute. It also avoids manipulating large matrices into a perfect square form. Expanding \(E(\mathbf{w})\) gives \[ E(\mathbf{w}) = \frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{t}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\mathbf{t} - \mathbf{t}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\mathbf{t} + \mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w}). \]

Since \(\mathbf{t}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w}\) is a scalar, it equals its transpose \(\mathbf{w}^T\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\mathbf{t}\). Two rules of matrix calculus give the gradient. For a constant vector \(\mathbf{a}\), the gradient of \(\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{w}\) is \(\mathbf{a}\). For a symmetric matrix \(\mathbf{A}\), the gradient of \(\mathbf{w}^T\mathbf{A}\mathbf{w}\) is \(2\mathbf{A}\mathbf{w}\). The matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\) is symmetric because \(\mathbf{S}^{-1}\) is diagonal. Taking the derivative with respect to \(\mathbf{w}\) with these rules gives \[ \nabla_\mathbf{w} E(\mathbf{w}) = -\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\mathbf{t} + \boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w} = -\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}(\mathbf{t} - \boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w}). \]

Here the nabla symbol \(\nabla_\mathbf{w}\) is the gradient operator with respect to the vector \(\mathbf{w}\). It gives a vector of the partial derivatives of \(E(\mathbf{w})\) with respect to each component of \(\mathbf{w}\). For a vector \(\mathbf{w} = (w_0, w_1, \ldots, w_{M-1})^T\), the gradient is \[ \nabla_\mathbf{w} E(\mathbf{w}) = \left(\frac{\partial E}{\partial w_0}, \frac{\partial E}{\partial w_1}, \ldots, \frac{\partial E}{\partial w_{M-1}}\right)^T. \]

This gradient depends on \(\mathbf{w}\). At the minimum of \(E(\mathbf{w})\), which is the maximum of the likelihood, it must equal zero. Setting \(\nabla_\mathbf{w} E(\mathbf{w}) = 0\) gives \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\mathbf{w} = \boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\mathbf{t}\). Solving for \(\mathbf{w}\) gives the maximum likelihood estimate \[ \mathbf{w}_{\text{ML}} = (\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\mathbf{t}. \tag{4.30} \]

For homogeneous noise, where \(\sigma_i = \sigma\) for all \(i\), the matrix \(\mathbf{S}\) simplifies to \(\sigma^2\mathrm{Id}\), where \(\mathrm{Id}\) is the identity matrix. Substituting this into our solution gives \[\begin{aligned} \mathbf{w}_{\text{ML}} &= (\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T(\sigma^2\mathrm{Id})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T(\sigma^2\mathrm{Id})^{-1}\mathbf{t} \\ &= (\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\mathrm{Id}\boldsymbol{\Phi})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\mathrm{Id}\mathbf{t} \\ &= (\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\boldsymbol{\Phi})^{-1}\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{t} \\ &= \sigma^2(\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\boldsymbol{\Phi})^{-1}\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{t} \\ &= (\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\boldsymbol{\Phi})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{t}. \end{aligned}\]This simplified form is the ordinary least squares solution \[ \mathbf{w}_{\text{ML}} = (\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\boldsymbol{\Phi})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{t}. \] The general weighted solution thus reduces to the unweighted case when the measurement uncertainties are uniform.

As a concrete example, consider fitting a straight line \(y = mx + b\) to data points \((x_i, y_i)\). For this model, \(\mathbf{w} = (b,m)^T\) holds the intercept and slope, and \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\) is an \(N \times 2\) matrix whose rows are \((1, x_i)\). The vector \(\mathbf{t}\) holds the observed \(y\) values. The matrix products in the solution then reduce to simple sums over the data \[ \boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\boldsymbol{\Phi} = \begin{pmatrix} N & \sum x_i \\ \sum x_i & \sum x_i^2 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{t} = \begin{pmatrix} \sum y_i \\ \sum x_iy_i \end{pmatrix}. \] For uniform uncertainties, inverting this \(2 \times 2\) matrix gives the familiar formulas \[ m = \frac{N\sum x_iy_i - (\sum x_i)(\sum y_i)}{N\sum x_i^2 - (\sum x_i)^2}, \quad b = \frac{\sum y_i - m\sum x_i}{N}. \]

When the measurement uncertainties \(\sigma_i\) vary between points, the weighted least squares solution instead gives \[ m = \frac{\sum \omega_ix_iy_i - (\sum \omega_ix_i)(\sum \omega_iy_i)/\Omega}{\sum \omega_ix_i^2 - (\sum \omega_ix_i)^2/\Omega}, \quad b = \frac{\sum \omega_iy_i - m\sum \omega_ix_i}{\Omega}, \] where \(\omega_i = 1/\sigma_i^2\) and \(\Omega = \sum \omega_i\). This weights more precise measurements (smaller \(\sigma_i\)) more heavily in the fit.

Properties of the Solution

This analytical solution has several properties that make linear regression useful in astronomy. First, it gives an exact solution without iterative numerical optimization, even with heterogeneous measurement uncertainties. Second, its mathematical form holds whatever the dimensionality of the feature space, as long as the matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{S}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}\) can be inverted. The inverse exists only when the columns of \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\) are linearly independent, which requires \(N \ge M\). This is especially useful for high-dimensional astronomical data, such as spectroscopic observations where each spectrum contains thousands of flux measurements at different wavelengths.

The cost of the computation also scales well with the size of the dataset. The matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\) is \(M \times N\), \(\mathbf{S}^{-1}\) is \(N \times N\), and \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\) is \(N \times M\), so their product is an \(M \times M\) matrix that we must invert. Since \(\mathbf{S}\) is diagonal, forming this product takes a number of operations proportional to \(NM^2\), which grows only linearly with the number of data points. The inversion takes a number of operations proportional to \(M^3\). This depends on the number of features \(M\) and not on the number of data points. With millions of data points and only a few hundred features, for example, both steps remain feasible.

4.5 Noise Parameter Estimation

So far we have treated the measurement uncertainties \(\sigma_i\) as known. In many astronomical applications, however, we must estimate them from the data. In spectroscopy, for example, the quoted instrumental uncertainties may miss systematic effects from sky subtraction or flux calibration. In photometric time series, the formal uncertainties often underestimate the true scatter because of unmodeled stellar variability or atmospheric effects.

In some cases, the spread in the data also shows physically meaningful variation as well as measurement error. The intrinsic dispersion in a mass-metallicity relation, for example, could indicate real diversity in galaxy evolution histories. Scatter in a period-luminosity relation might reveal real differences in stellar properties. Modeling this intrinsic scatter properly can give useful physical insight beyond accounting for the measurement uncertainties.

From a maximum likelihood perspective, we can include the measurement uncertainties as additional model parameters. If we denote the model parameters by \(\mathbf{w}\) and the measurement uncertainties by \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\), we maximize \(p(\mathbf{t}|\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{w}, \boldsymbol{\sigma})\) with respect to both \(\mathbf{w}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\) simultaneously. Both the model parameters and the noise characteristics shape the distribution of the observed data.

Figure 4.2 shows that the estimate of the measurement uncertainties matters for the likelihood. When the uncertainties are underestimated (panel a), many data points fall outside the predicted uncertainty bands. Each such point contributes a small likelihood term \(\mathcal{N}(t_i|y(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{w}), \sigma^2)\) because the Gaussian falls off rapidly, so the overall likelihood is low. When the uncertainties are overestimated (panel c), the Gaussians are very broad, and more points fall within the expected range. The prefactor \(1/\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}\) then becomes very small and again lowers the overall likelihood. The maximum likelihood value of \(\sigma\) lies close to the choice in panel (b), where these two effects balance.

We must model the uncertainty with care. Letting each data point have its own independent uncertainty \(\sigma_i\) would add as many parameters as there are data points and leave the model ill-constrained. To see why, recall that for a Gaussian likelihood each data point contributes a term \((t_i - y_i)^2/\sigma_i^2\) to \(\chi^2\). If each \(\sigma_i\) could vary independently, setting \(\sigma_i = |t_i - y_i|\) would give \(\chi^2 = N\) for any model parameters. Each point would then contribute exactly 1, however well or poorly the model fits the data. We could not compare model fits meaningfully, and the model would have no predictive power, because the uncertainties would adjust to fit any predictions.

Estimating a Single Noise Level

To make the problem well defined, we therefore need a noise model with fewer parameters than data points. We might assume, for instance, that the measurement uncertainty varies smoothly with the input features. As an illustration, we consider the simplest scenario, a homogeneous but unknown measurement uncertainty, where all measurements share the same unknown \(\sigma\).

We write the log-likelihood with the precision \(\beta = 1/\sigma^2\) to simplify the derivation \[ \ln p(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{w}, \beta) = \frac{N}{2} \ln \beta - \frac{N}{2} \ln(2\pi) - \frac{\beta}{2} \sum_{i=1}^N (t_i - \mathbf{w}^T \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_i))^2. \]

Previously, we treated \(\sigma\) as a fixed, known quantity while optimizing for \(\mathbf{w}\). Now we treat \(\sigma\) as another parameter of the model, just like \(\mathbf{w}\).

To find the optimal value of \(\beta\), we follow the same approach as for \(\mathbf{w}\). We differentiate the log-likelihood with respect to \(\beta\) and set the result to zero \[ \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta} \ln p(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{w}, \beta) = \frac{N}{2\beta} - \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^N (t_i - \mathbf{w}^T \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_i))^2 = 0. \]Solving for \(\beta\) and converting back to \(\sigma^2\) gives \[ \frac{1}{\beta_{\text{ML}}} = \sigma^2_{\text{ML}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N (t_i - \mathbf{w}^T \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_i))^2. \]

This equation gives an intuitive estimate of the measurement variance, the average of the squared residuals between the observations and the model predictions. If the model fits the data well, the remaining discrepancies between predictions and observations should reflect the underlying measurement noise. Averaging the squared residuals then estimates the typical squared deviation (variance) in the measurements. This is analogous to estimating the uncertainty from repeated measurements of one quantity, where we look at the scatter around the mean. Here we compare with the model predictions instead of a mean, but the principle is the same. Small residuals suggest precise measurements (small \(\sigma^2\)), and larger residuals indicate more uncertain ones (large \(\sigma^2\)).

Estimating the Weights and the Noise Together

However, the likelihood \(p(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{w}, \beta)\) depends jointly on \(\mathbf{w}\) and \(\beta\). To find the true maximum likelihood solution, we need to maximize over both parameters simultaneously. In mathematical terms, we seek \[ (\mathbf{w}_{\text{ML}}, \beta_{\text{ML}}) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{w}, \beta} p(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{w}, \beta). \]

Our problem has a special structure that makes this tractable. We have already shown that for any fixed \(\beta\) we can find \(\mathbf{w}_{\text{ML}}(\beta)\) analytically. Similarly, for any fixed \(\mathbf{w}\) we can find \(\beta_{\text{ML}}(\mathbf{w})\) analytically. This suggests the following iterative approach.

  1. Start with an initial guess for \(\beta\)

  2. Find \(\mathbf{w}_{\text{ML}}(\beta)\) with the least squares solution

  3. Use this \(\mathbf{w}_{\text{ML}}(\beta)\) to find \(\beta_{\text{ML}}(\mathbf{w})\) with the variance estimation formula

  4. Repeat steps 2-3 until convergence, meaning until \(\mathbf{w}\) and \(\beta\) stop changing

In this specific case, the iteration converges whatever the initial guess for \(\beta\). To see why, we examine the structure of the log-likelihood \[ \ln p(\mathbf{t} | \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{w}, \beta) = \frac{N}{2} \ln \beta - \frac{N}{2} \ln(2\pi) - \frac{\beta}{2} \sum_{i=1}^N (t_i - \mathbf{w}^T \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_i))^2. \]

First, each step of the iteration has a single best answer. With \(\sigma^2\) fixed, the exponent contains squared distances between the predictions and the observations. The log-likelihood is therefore concave in \(\mathbf{w}\) and has a single peak. Away from the peak, the likelihood falls off as a Gaussian.

Similarly, varying \(\sigma^2\) while holding \(\mathbf{w}\) fixed gives another single peak. A very small \(\sigma^2\) makes the Gaussians too narrow, so points that do not match the predictions exactly get exponentially small likelihoods. A very large \(\sigma^2\) makes the Gaussians too wide, and the normalization term \(1/\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}\) drives the likelihood toward zero. The likelihood must therefore peak at an intermediate value where these competing effects balance.

The two parameters are also connected in a simple way. The optimal \(\mathbf{w}_{\text{ML}}\) depends only on the relative weighting of the squared residuals, which is independent of the scale of \(\beta\). For homogeneous noise, the best \(\mathbf{w}\) is therefore the same for every \(\beta\), so the global maximum must have \(\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{w}_{\text{ML}}\). The optimal \(\beta\) then follows directly from this \(\mathbf{w}\), so one pass through steps 2 and 3 reaches the single global maximum. This takes two steps, as Figure 4.3 shows.

Putting these results together, we obtain the maximum likelihood solution in a simple two-step process. First, we estimate \(\mathbf{w}_{\text{ML}}\) with the least squares solution \[ \mathbf{w}_{\text{ML}} = (\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\boldsymbol{\Phi})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{t}. \]Then, using this \(\mathbf{w}_{\text{ML}}\), we compute \(\sigma^2_{\text{ML}}\) directly as \[ \sigma^2_{\text{ML}} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N (t_i - \mathbf{w}_{\text{ML}}^T \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}_i))^2. \]This estimate of \(\sigma^2\) is the average squared deviation between the observations and the model predictions. It gives the typical size of the noise in our data, whether instrumental or intrinsic. This assumes that the residual differences come mainly from noise rather than from model inadequacies, which is reasonable for a model that fits well.

A common case in astronomy has known measurement uncertainties \(\sigma_i\) and an intrinsic scatter \(\sigma_{\rm int}\) that we must estimate. The total variance of point \(i\) is then \(\sigma_i^2 + \sigma_{\rm int}^2\). We replace \(\sigma_i^2\) by this sum in the heterogeneous log-likelihood and maximize over \(\mathbf{w}\) and \(\sigma_{\rm int}\). For a fixed \(\sigma_{\rm int}\), the weights are \(1/(\sigma_i^2 + \sigma_{\rm int}^2)\), and \(\mathbf{w}\) follows from weighted least squares. For a fixed \(\mathbf{w}\), \(\sigma_{\rm int}\) has no closed form, so we alternate the two steps or optimize numerically. If the known uncertainties explain the scatter, the maximum lies at \(\sigma_{\rm int} = 0\).

4.6 Limitations of Maximum Likelihood Approach

Maximum likelihood estimation gives a well-defined way to find the best model parameters and even to estimate the measurement uncertainties. It also has three serious limitations.

The first and most critical limitation is that MLE alone reports a best-fit model, which falls short of a basic principle of science. In science, we want predictive models and also a clear understanding of their uncertainties and limits. We need the uncertainty of the model parameters and of the predictions we make with them.

When we compute \(\mathbf{w}_{\text{ML}}\), we obtain a single point estimate, our best guess for the model parameters. This estimate does not tell us how confident we should be in it. Are the parameters well constrained by the data, or might a wide range of values be equally plausible? Without uncertainty quantification, we cannot answer these questions.

Consider our earlier M-\(\sigma\) relation example. Suppose we find \(\gamma = 4.0\) for the power-law index. MLE alone does not tell us whether the data constrain this value to within \(\pm 0.1\) or allow a range from \(3.0\) to \(5.0\). We need this uncertainty to compare our results with theoretical predictions or with measurements from other studies.

Residuals and goodness-of-fit statistics tell us how well the model fits, but they do not give uncertainties on the parameters. Without them, we cannot propagate errors through later calculations or compare models with different numbers of parameters. Other tools can add them, such as the bootstrap of Chapter 3, which resamples the data. Such tools are extra steps on top of the point estimate. The bootstrap, for example, has practical limits that Chapter 5 discusses.

The second limitation is that MLE assumes no prior knowledge and treats the data alone as sufficient to determine the parameters. In astronomy, we often have prior knowledge that could improve our estimates. We might know physical constraints on the parameter values, or have results from previous studies that suggest likely ranges. In stellar astrophysics, for example, stellar masses must be positive and typically fall within ranges set by stellar evolution theory. In cosmology, nucleosynthesis or structure formation can limit the parameter ranges. MLE has no way to include such knowledge.

The third limitation is that MLE does not guard against overfitting on its own. It can produce models that fit the training data well but generalize poorly to new observations. Overfitting is most likely when there are nearly as many parameters as data points, or when the basis functions \(\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})\) can follow very complex curves. Our analytical solutions only find the parameters that best explain the observed data. They do not check how well the predictions hold for new data.

The first two limitations need a more complete approach, which we introduce at the end of this chapter. For the third, the next section shows how to detect overfitting with test data.

4.7 Model Evaluation and Cross-Validation

This section addresses the third limitation of maximum likelihood, overfitting. Overfitting can arise with other approaches too. Each model needs a choice of complexity, such as the number of basis functions, and a test of whether it generalizes. Cross-validation is a standard tool for model evaluation and selection, and we illustrate it with linear regression.

A central question in machine learning is what makes a good model. We explore it with polynomial regression. Recall from our discussion of basis functions that we can write a linear regression model as \[ y(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{w}) = \sum_{j=0}^{M-1} w_j \cdot \phi_j(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{w}^T \boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x}). \]

For polynomial regression, we choose polynomial basis functions \(\phi_0(x) = 1\), \(\phi_1(x) = x\), \(\phi_2(x) = x^2\), and so on. This gives \[ y(x, \mathbf{w}) = w_0 + w_1x + w_2x^2 + \ldots + w_{M-1}x^{M-1}, \] where the weights \(\mathbf{w}\) come from our maximum likelihood solution \(\mathbf{w}_{\text{ML}} = (\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\boldsymbol{\Phi})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{t}\). This is the linear regression we derived, with polynomial basis functions. This choice of transformations is called feature engineering.

How many polynomial terms should the basis functions \(\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})\) include? We choose the dimension \(M\) of the feature space, and so the structure of the design matrix \(\boldsymbol{\Phi}\). This question is an example of the bias-variance tradeoff, which we explain below. It also connects to the overfitting limitation of maximum likelihood.

We can measure how well the model does with the mean squared error \[ \text{MSE} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N(t_i - y(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{w}))^2. \] This is the squared-error loss that follows from our homoscedastic Gaussian noise assumption in maximum likelihood estimation.

Underfitting and Overfitting

Modeling uses prior knowledge and assumptions, and learning finds patterns in data. Machine learning balances the two. As we add polynomial basis functions, we increase the complexity of the feature space, and we see three regimes (Figure 4.4).

First, underfitting occurs when the basis functions are too limited to follow the patterns in the data. A purely linear model applied to a nonlinear astronomical relationship is an example. Second, in the optimal balance the model follows the true underlying relationship, and measurement noise has little effect on the fit. Finally, overfitting occurs when the feature space becomes so complex that the model fits the measurement noise instead of the signal.

Good models generalize to new observations, and this is what separates the three regimes. This principle is basic to scientific inference. Our models should make accurate predictions about future data, and low residuals on existing measurements are not enough.

Training and Test Sets

The solution is to split our dataset into separate portions. We use a training set to fit the model parameters. For each choice of basis functions, we apply our maximum likelihood solution \(\mathbf{w}_{\text{ML}} = (\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\boldsymbol{\Phi})^{-1}\boldsymbol{\Phi}^T\mathbf{t}\) to find the optimal weights. We hold out a test set during training to evaluate how well the model generalizes. We compute the mean squared error on each set, which gives the training error and the test error.

The test data played no role in the parameter estimation. The test error is therefore an unbiased estimate of how the model will do on future data.

This split shows why the errors on training and test data behave differently. On the training data, adding degrees of freedom (more polynomial basis functions) does not worsen the fit and usually improves it. With more terms, the larger feature space gives the maximum likelihood solution more freedom to reduce the training error. At some point, however, we begin to overfit the specific characteristics of the training set, even though the fit to the training data keeps improving.

When overfitting occurs, the model memorizes noise and peculiarities of the training data instead of the true underlying relationship. These noise patterns are artifacts of our particular measurements and say nothing about the physical system we are studying. They do not generalize to new observations, which leads to larger errors on the test set.

Figure 4.5 shows the result. The training error does not increase as we add basis functions, but the test error follows a U-shaped curve. With too few basis functions (underfitting), both errors are high because the model is too rigid. In the optimal regime, the test error reaches its minimum while the training error is already low. In the overfitting regime, the training error keeps decreasing while the test error increases.

The Bias-Variance Tradeoff

The bias-variance tradeoff explains this U-shape. Bias is the systematic error that remains when the model family cannot represent the true relationship. It is not the intercept \(w_0\), which we also called the bias term. A straight line fitted to a curved relation has high bias, and more data do not remove it. Variance measures how much the fitted curve changes from one training set to another. Each training set has its own measurement noise, so a model with many parameters gives a different curve for each set.

Low-order polynomials have high bias and low variance, so they underfit (orders 1 and 2 in Figure 4.4). High-order polynomials have low bias and high variance, so they overfit (order 15). Higher orders lower the bias and raise the variance. The test error depends on both, so it is lowest at an intermediate order (order 5 in Figure 4.5).

More complex models fit the training data better but generalize worse. This tension is basic to machine learning. Recent work on neural networks has challenged this picture. The “double descent” phenomenon shows that highly overparameterized models can sometimes generalize better than expected, a topic we explore in Chapter 15. Such a model has more parameters than data points. For polynomial regression and many classical methods, however, the U-shaped test error curve remains standard.

Three-Way Data Splitting

For a more careful procedure, we can use a three-way split. The training set fits the weight vector \(\mathbf{w}\) with our maximum likelihood solution for each choice of basis functions. The validation set determines the dimensionality of the feature space, meaning how many polynomial terms to include in \(\boldsymbol{\phi}(\mathbf{x})\). The test set then gives a final evaluation of the chosen model on unseen data. Model selection thus rests on the validation set, and the test set gives an unbiased estimate of how well the model generalizes.

There is a tension between having enough training data for reliable parameter estimation and enough validation or test data for trustworthy evaluation. A common split uses 60% of the data for training, 20% for validation, and 20% for testing. The proportions should depend on the total dataset size and the specific problem.

In astronomy, data can be scarce, so we often use only training and test sets. This is a compromise, because model selection then depends on the test set. It is still a reasonable balance between statistical accuracy and practical constraints.

Cross-Validation for Limited Data

When datasets are small, cross-validation is an alternative that uses the available data more efficiently. In Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV), we apply our maximum likelihood solution \(N\) times. Each time, we train on \(N-1\) observations and hold out the remaining one as the test set. Each observation is held out exactly once, and we average the test errors to estimate how well the model predicts.

This approach makes full use of the data, since nearly all observations train each model. It also gives \(N\) estimates of how well the model generalizes. However, LOOCV usually trains \(N\) models, which can be slow. Because each test set has only one observation, individual test results can be noisy. The training sets differ by one observation, so the \(N\) results are highly correlated. Their average can vary widely between datasets.

K-fold cross-validation is a practical compromise. It divides the data into \(K\) folds, trains on \(K-1\) folds, and tests on the remaining fold. We rotate through the folds and average the test errors. This reduces computation while keeping many advantages of LOOCV.

Cross-validation in astronomy often needs care with the structure of the data. For time-series observations, random splitting can leak information from the future into predictions of the past. Time-aware splitting may be more appropriate. When observations cluster spatially, random splitting may not test predictions for new regions of the sky. Selection effects and systematic uncertainties also affect how we interpret the results.

Cross-validation is a practical tool for any fit. Later chapters give other ways to compare models, such as information criteria for mixture models in Chapter 11. Information criteria balance how well a model fits against its number of parameters. Cross-validation only checks generalization. It gives no parameter uncertainties and ignores priors.

A more complete approach is Bayesian inference. MLE asks which parameter values best explain the observed data. Bayesian inference treats the parameters as random variables and asks for their complete probability distribution, given the data and our prior knowledge. Instead of a point estimate like \(\mathbf{w}_{\text{ML}}\), it gives the posterior distribution \(p(\mathbf{w}|\mathbf{t})\). The posterior gives the uncertainties in the model parameters in one calculation, with no separate recipe. We then understand the precision and limits of our results.

The posterior also gives predictions with uncertainty estimates, through the posterior predictive distribution (Section 5.7), the distribution of a new observation given our data. It separates aleatoric uncertainty, the randomness of the measurements, from epistemic uncertainty, our limited knowledge of the parameters (Section 3.8). Bayesian inference includes prior knowledge formally, so we can build on previous results and theoretical constraints. The same priors act as regularization, a penalty on large parameter values that guards against overfitting. The width of the prior is a hyperparameter, and we still set it on validation data (Section 4.7). In astronomy, understanding the uncertainties is often as important as the estimates themselves, and Chapter 5 develops this approach.

4.8 Tutorials: Stellar Spectra and Calibration

Two tutorials apply the least squares fit of this chapter to astronomy. The first predicts the temperature of a star from its spectrum, with a prior and test stars. The second removes instrumental and atmospheric effects from radial velocities, with the bootstrap. The full tutorials can be found at https://tingyuansen.github.io/statml/ as 4a and 4b.

Stellar Temperatures from Spectra

A spectroscopic survey such as APOGEE records the infrared spectra of hundreds of thousands of stars. The strength of the absorption lines in a spectrum depends on the temperature, the gravity and the composition of the stellar atmosphere. Temperature, for example, sets the ionization state of the atoms and so the strength of their lines. Such parameters for many stars map the chemistry of the Milky Way. The lines are deeper in the spectra of cooler stars (Figure 4.6a).

Linear regression predicts the temperature from the spectrum. The flux at each wavelength is a feature, and the temperature is the quantity to predict. The prediction is a weighted sum of the fluxes, with a weight for each wavelength. The analytical solution of Section 4.4 gives these weights without iteration. The training stars have temperatures from the survey pipeline, and the fitted model predicts the temperatures of other stars from their spectra.

A spectrum has so many wavelengths that the model has almost as many weights as there are training stars. With so many weights, the model can follow each training star, including its noise. Section 4.6 explains why maximum likelihood does not guard against overfitting here. We hold out some stars as test stars, as in Section 4.7. The maximum likelihood fit matches the training stars almost exactly but predicts the test stars less well (Figure 4.6b).

The remedy is a prior on the weights that makes large values unlikely. As the end of Section 4.7 explains, such a prior discourages large weights, which is called regularization. In practice, a third group of stars, the validation stars, sets how much large weights are discouraged. The test stars then remain an unbiased check (Section 4.7). The regularized fit predicts the test stars better (Figure 4.6b). Regularization guards against overfitting, especially with many input features (Section 4.7).

Calibrating Telescope Measurements

Many planets are found through the tiny wobbles that they cause in their host stars. The radial velocities of the host stars, their velocities along the line of sight, must be very precise. At this precision the measured velocity depends on the observing conditions. The changes from the instrument and the atmosphere are called systematic effects. Uncorrected, they can exceed the wobbles, so they must be removed.

In the simulation we assume that four recorded conditions change the velocity, and a real instrument has many more. The zenith angle is the angle of the star from the vertical, and a star far from the vertical is seen through more air. A change of temperature expands the optics, and humidity changes the refractive index of the air. The instrument itself drifts during the night. A standard star has a constant velocity, so observing it under changing conditions shows how large these effects are (Figure 4.7a).

We treat calibration as a linear regression. The recorded conditions are the features, and the weights say how much each condition changes the velocity. The velocity of the star does not change from one observation to the next, but the conditions do. The fit therefore treats the part that varies with the conditions as the instrument and the constant part as the star. The constant part is the intercept (Section 4.4). After we subtract the part that the conditions explain, the velocities of the simulated observations scatter around the true value by the noise (Figure 4.7b).

Scaled by how much each condition varies, the fitted weights also show which condition matters most. This guides the design of the instrument and the planning of observations. Real observations differ in quality, because clouds and poor seeing add noise. Measurements with unequal uncertainties enter through the weighted fit of Section 4.3, which counts the noisy measurements less. We also need the uncertainty of the fitted velocity. The bootstrap of Section 3.7 shows how it shrinks with the number of observations, and so how much telescope time a calibration needs.

The same idea scales to a network of telescopes. Each telescope responds differently to the conditions, but they observe the same standard stars. After calibration, their measurements must agree on the velocity of each star. These common stars calibrate the whole network in one regression with a larger design matrix. The method applies to measurements whose systematic effects depend on recorded quantities, such as the dimming of starlight by the atmosphere at large zenith angles. Surveys that combine telescopes need such cross-calibration to compare their measurements.

Linear models remain useful in astronomy despite their simplicity, especially with well-chosen features. Transformations such as logarithms and polynomials let a model that is linear in its weights describe many nonlinear relations (Section 4.2). The two tutorials use the measurements themselves as features, the flux at each wavelength and the observing conditions. Three tools make such a fit trustworthy. Test stars show how well the model predicts new data, a prior limits overfitting, and the bootstrap gives uncertainties.

Further Reading

Gauss (1823) gave an account of the theory of least squares. Its Gauss-Markov theorem shows that least squares has the lowest variance among unbiased linear estimators. Bevington (1969) is a widely used reference on weighted least squares and error analysis in the physical sciences. Faber and Jackson (1976) found that the luminosity of elliptical galaxies scales roughly with the fourth power of the velocity dispersion. Tully and Fisher (1977) related the luminosity of spiral galaxies to the width of their neutral hydrogen line, a proxy for rotation velocity. Ferrarese and Merritt (2000) and Gebhardt et al. (2000) found tight correlations between supermassive black hole masses and the velocity dispersions of their host galaxies. The intrinsic scatter is small. Kennicutt (1998) characterized the star formation law that relates gas density to star formation rate. Isobe et al. (1990) compared regression methods for astronomical data. Akritas and Bershady (1996) developed an estimator for correlated errors, unequal uncertainties and intrinsic scatter. Stone (1974) used cross-validation to choose among statistical predictors and to test them.
